paragraphs: A rich vein was struck at the Laurion mines southeast of Athens around 483 BCE, worked by thousands of enslaved labourers driven through cramped tunnels. The Athenian assembly debated simply dividing the windfall among citizens, but Themistocles argued for spending it on ships instead.

That decision funded roughly 200 triremes, the fleet that met the Persian navy at Salamis in 480 BCE and won. Laurion's silver kept flowing into Athenian coinage for decades afterward, underwriting the fleet and public works that made Athens the dominant sea power of the Aegean.

The Athenian tetradrachm carried Athena's head on one side and her owl on the other, struck in silver from around 510 BCE onward. Its weight and purity stayed reliable for generations, which mattered more to a foreign merchant than any claim about who issued it, and the coin became the closest thing the ancient Mediterranean had to a reserve currency.

Egyptian and Levantine mints struck their own close copies of the owl design well outside Athenian territory, simply because merchants trusted the pattern. The silver came largely from the state-owned mines at Laurion, so a coin stamped with a bird effectively advertised the reliability of Athens' bullion supply.

The United Provinces had no fewer than fourteen mints and a flood of foreign coin circulating alongside them, so a merchant could rarely be sure what a coin in their hand was actually worth. Amsterdam's city council set up the Wisselbank in 1609 to fix that, letting merchants deposit bullion and coin of varying quality in exchange for a standardised account balance.

Those balances, not coin, became the currency traders actually used to settle bills, since a Wisselbank guilder was reliably worth the same amount regardless of whose mint had struck the metal behind it. The bank never issued paper notes, but it pioneered the idea of money as an entry in a ledger, which did more to make Amsterdam a financial capital than any coin it held in its vaults.

On 16 September 1992 the Bank of England raised interest rates twice in a single day, to 12 percent and then a promised 15, trying to hold the pound above its floor in Europe's Exchange Rate Mechanism. Traders, George Soros most famously, had bet heavily that sterling could not stay there, and they were right.

By evening Chancellor Norman Lamont announced Britain's withdrawal from the mechanism, and the pound fell freely against the mark. The Treasury later estimated the defence had cost billions of pounds in reserves and failed intervention, and Soros's fund alone is reported to have made roughly a billion dollars from the single day's trading.

Constantine issued the solidus around 312, a gold coin struck at 72 to the Roman pound, deliberately shielded from the debasement that had gutted the silver denarius over the previous century. Where earlier emperors had quietly thinned their coinage to cover costs, the solidus held its weight and purity by policy, coin after coin, reign after reign.

It worked for an unusually long time. The solidus stayed close to its original standard for roughly seven centuries, financing Byzantine trade from Ravenna to India, and its Arabic name, the dinar of gold merchants referenced by weight, and its later descendant, the shilling abbreviation 's', both trace back to this one coin's stability.

Hammurabi's code capped what a Babylonian lender could charge: about 33 percent a year on grain loans and 20 percent on silver, cut into stone on a black basalt pillar for anyone to read. Charge more, and the code let the debtor void the loan outright, a remedy sharper than most modern usury law offers.

The pillar was carried off as war booty to Susa in the twelfth century BCE, which is where French archaeologists found it in 1901, broken into three pieces. Its 282 laws cover far more than interest, but the lending rules survive as one of the earliest attempts to write a ceiling into the price of borrowing money.

Contactless bank cards use the same radio chip found in transit passes, letting a shopper tap near a reader instead of inserting a card and typing a code. Barclaycard issued Britain's first contactless bank card in 2007, and transport operators, London's Oyster network among the earliest, had already proven the technology worked at speed for years before that.

Adoption crept along for a decade until issuers raised the tap limit and card networks pushed the format harder, then jumped again once the COVID-19 pandemic made shoppers wary of touching a shared keypad. By the early 2020s contactless had overtaken chip-and-pin as the routine way to pay for small purchases across much of Europe.

The Second Continental Congress had no power to tax, so from 1775 it paid for the war against Britain by printing paper Continentals, authorising roughly 241 million dollars in bills of credit over four years while individual states issued their own currencies alongside them. Nothing backed the notes but a promise that Congress could not keep.

By early 1781, depreciation had reached seventy-five to one in most states and over two hundred to one in North Carolina; a dollar that bought a silver dollar's worth of goods in 1775 was worth about two and a half cents. Not worth a Continental became a common phrase for anything worthless, and the collapse left Americans deeply wary of paper money for a generation afterward.

On 15 February 1971, Decimal Day, Britain replaced a system in which twelve pence made a shilling and twenty shillings made a pound with a single pound divided into one hundred new pence. Preparation had run for years: new coins circulated alongside old ones from 1968, and banks closed for four days around the changeover to convert accounts.

Shops had to reprice everything, and some retailers were accused of rounding prices up under cover of the confusion, feeding public grumbling about a hidden price rise. Even so, the switch went through with far less disruption than officials had feared, and within months the old shillings and pre-decimal pennies had largely vanished from tills.

The Nasdaq index peaked on 10 March 2000 at over 5,000, propped up by companies that had never turned a profit but had a dot-com in their name and a splashy Super Bowl advert to their name. Within weeks the index began sliding as investors who had priced in endless growth started asking when the growth would actually arrive.

It took two and a half years for the Nasdaq to bottom out, down roughly 78 percent from its peak, taking pets.com, Webvan and hundreds of smaller ventures with it. The companies that survived, among them Amazon and eBay, had spent the boom building something a customer could actually use rather than just a valuation.

Luca Pacioli did not invent double-entry bookkeeping. Venetian merchants had used it for generations before he wrote a word; his contribution in 1494 was to print it. Summa de Arithmetica, Geometria, Proportioni et Proportionalita, printed in Venice by Paganino de Paganini, included a twenty-seven-page section called Particularis de Computis et Scripturis that laid out the method step by step.

Pacioli called it the Method of Venice and wrote it in Italian rather than Latin, aiming it squarely at working merchants rather than scholars. That choice of audience is why the technique spread across Italy and then Europe: a friar with no trading business of his own had written the manual that let anyone else's books balance.

Egyptian farmers did not keep their surplus wheat at home. It went into state granaries, where a scribe weighed and logged it and issued a written receipt. That receipt, not the grain itself, could then be used to pay a debt, buy goods, or settle taxes, because the grain sitting in the granary backed it.

By the Ptolemaic period, around the third century BCE, these granaries had become a network with something close to a central accounting office in Alexandria, transferring grain credits between depositors the way a bank transfers coin. It let value move across the country without moving a single sack of wheat.

Roger of Salisbury organised England's exchequer as a distinct department under Henry I around 1110, built to audit sheriffs who collected the crown's revenue from every shire. Officials sat around a table covered in a cloth marked out in squares, using counters moved across it like an abacus to check accounts, which is where the department took its name.

Debts and receipts were also recorded on tally sticks, notched wooden rods split lengthwise so the creditor and debtor each held a matching half that could be checked against the other. The system, cloth and sticks together, ran English royal accounting for centuries; the sticks themselves were not formally abandoned until the early nineteenth century.

Henry II reissued English silver coinage in 1158 with the Tealby penny, named centuries later for a hoard dug up at Tealby in Lincolnshire in 1807. It replaced a coinage badly debased during the civil war years known as the Anarchy, when barons and rival claimants had struck their own inconsistent pennies across the country.

The Tealby standard held roughly 240 pennies to a pound of silver, the ratio that gave the pound sterling its name and its arithmetic, twenty shillings and twelve pence to the shilling, a system England kept until decimalisation in 1971. Henry replaced the Tealby design itself in 1180 with the more uniform Short Cross penny, but the underlying weight standard he set carried on.

Ethereum went live on 30 July 2015, built by programmer Vitalik Buterin and a small team who wanted a blockchain that did more than track a currency. Bitcoin's ledger could only record who owned what; Ethereum let anyone deploy code, called a smart contract, that ran automatically whenever its conditions were met, with no bank or clearing house in between.

That capability spawned an entire industry of tokens, decentralised exchanges and lending platforms built on top of Ethereum rather than competing with it. It also produced early disasters, including a 2016 hack of a fund called the DAO that forced the network to split in two rather than let stolen funds stand.

Franklin Roosevelt signed Executive Order 6102 on 5 April 1933, ordering Americans to hand over gold coin, gold bullion and gold certificates above a small allowance to Federal Reserve banks, in exchange for paper dollars at the fixed rate of just over twenty dollars an ounce. Collectible and rare coins were exempted, which is how some gold legally stayed in private hands.

The order was meant to stop hoarding and let the Treasury expand the money supply during the Depression. Months later Congress raised the official gold price to thirty-five dollars an ounce, a devaluation that instantly profited the government on the gold it had just collected. Americans could not legally own gold bullion again until the ban was lifted in 1974.

William Pitt the Younger introduced the tax in December 1798, effective from 1799, to pay for the war against France, and he called it temporary. Rates ran on a sliding scale up to ten percent on incomes above sixty pounds a year, a threshold that spared most labourers while reaching merchants and landowners.

Pitt's government promised the tax would end with the war. It was repealed in 1802 after the Peace of Amiens, revived the next year when fighting resumed, and abolished again in 1816 after Waterloo, with Parliament ordering the tax records burned. A peacetime version returned permanently in 1842 under Robert Peel.

Richard Ketley ran the Golden Cross inn on Snow Hill in Birmingham, and in 1775 he turned his pub into the meeting place for what became the world's first building society. Members paid regular subscriptions into a shared fund, and when enough had accumulated, the society drew lots to decide which member's house got built or bought next.

Almost nothing survives of Ketley's society beyond three newspaper advertisements from 1778 and 1779 offering shares in it, and it was terminating rather than permanent: once every member had a home, the society wound itself up. That modest, self-liquidating model spread through the Midlands and the North and, by 1910, had grown into more than 1,700 societies with over 600,000 members across Britain.

The earliest surviving English cheque was written by the merchant Nicholas Vanacker, made payable to a Mr Delboe for four hundred pounds and dated 16 February 1659 by the calendar then in use, drawn on the London bankers Robert Clayton and John Morris. Bills of exchange for trade had existed for centuries, but this was something narrower: an instruction to a banker to pay a named third party from the writer's own account.

Goldsmith-bankers like Clayton and Morris had begun holding deposits and issuing these written instructions as a convenience for regular customers rather than as a public product. Surviving examples from the Vanacker family span several years either side of 1659, suggesting the practice was already becoming routine among London's merchant class before anyone thought to record who did it first.

Bank of America mailed unsolicited cards to sixty thousand residents of Fresno, California, in September 1958, a launch bankers later called the Fresno Drop. Recipients had not applied for the cards or the credit lines attached to them, and the bank simply activated the accounts unless someone objected.

The rollout was chaotic: fraud and unpaid balances piled up faster than the bank could track them, and losses were heavy in the first years. BankAmericard survived the mess, expanded state by state, and in 1976 was renamed Visa so that other banks could license the network without carrying Bank of America's name on their own cards.

The Bank of Delaware ran the first debit card pilot in 1966, decades before the term meant much to anyone. The card looked like a credit card and worked at the same terminals, but it drew straight from the holder's own account rather than creating a loan, which made merchants and regulators alike unsure how to treat it.

For years the idea went nowhere. Early cards worked only at automated teller machines, doing little beyond dispensing cash, and it took until the early 1990s for point-of-sale networks to catch up so a card could debit a checking account at a till. The 1966 pilot is remembered as the origin only in hindsight.

On 28 February 1957 the Soviet state bank moved roughly eight hundred thousand dollars out of its accounts in New York and into its own London branch. Moscow wanted dollars for trade but feared that money held directly inside the American banking system could be frozen in a crisis, a worry sharpened by watching Washington pressure Britain over Suez the previous year.

The dollars never left the American banking system in any physical sense; they simply became the legal property of a bank in London rather than one in New York. Other banks and companies followed the same logic through the late 1950s and 1960s, building a market in dollars held and lent entirely outside US borders, immune to American reserve rules, that grew into trillions.

The oldest surviving insurance contract comes from Genoa in 1347 and covers a ship called the Santa Clara. It is written as a maritime loan rather than a straightforward policy, because canon law forbade usury and this structure let merchants collect a fee for taking on risk without the transaction looking like interest.

Underwriters signed the document individually, each writing their name beside the share of the cargo's risk they were willing to accept, a habit that gave the word underwriter its literal meaning. The practice spread along Genoese and Venetian trade routes long before England had anything comparable, and Lloyd's coffee house was still three centuries away.

Massachusetts Bay's paper money was born out of a military failure. In August 1690 Sir William Phips led thirty-four ships and roughly two thousand men against Quebec, and returned with a battered fleet, no treasure and soldiers close to mutiny over unpaid wages, with the colony's treasury holding nowhere near enough coin to settle the debt.

On 10 December 1690 the General Court ordered the printing of bills of credit to pay the men, a promise from the government to redeem the paper for coin later out of future taxes. It was the first government-issued paper currency in the Western world, and it set a pattern other colonies would copy for the rest of the century, usually for the same reason: a war bill that specie could not cover.

A Sumerian loan tablet was a receipt with teeth. A scribe pressed the terms into wet clay with a reed stylus, both parties impressed their cylinder seals into the surface, and the tablet was baked or sun-dried into a record that could not be altered afterwards without the tampering showing.

Some loans carried interest rates around 20 percent, recorded in the same wedge-shaped script used for grain counts and temple inventories. These tablets are the earliest surviving written contracts, and archives of thousands of them, dug up largely intact from sites like Ur and Nippur, let historians trace household debt in a city four thousand years before double-entry bookkeeping existed.

Henry Duncan was the minister of the small parish of Ruthwell in Dumfriesshire, and he was troubled by how quickly poor relief could tip his labouring parishioners into permanent dependency. In 1810 he opened a bank in the rooms of the local friendly society, accepting deposits from one shilling up to ten pounds and paying interest on them.

The Ruthwell Parish Bank was not the first place ordinary people could save money, but it is generally credited as the first run on organised business principles rather than as charity. Duncan published the model and it spread quickly across Scotland and England as the savings bank movement. Ruthwell's own bank had modest success and was absorbed by a neighbouring bank in 1875.

Shareholders in the Dutch East India Company waited eight years for any return at all, and when it finally came in 1610 it was not cash but mace, the spice, valued at seventy-five percent of their original investment. Investors had been agitating loudly by then, including a campaign led by Isaac Le Maire, who had turned his frustration with the company into history's first known short sale of its stock.

A cash dividend did not follow until 1612. Together the 1610 and 1612 payouts totalled a remarkable one hundred and sixty-two and a half percent of capital invested, effectively repaying shareholders in full and then some for years of tied-up money. The mace dividend was clumsy, but it was the first time a public company had paid its shareholders anything at all.

The London Credit Exchange Company issued its first instruments on 1 January 1772, redeemable at listed correspondents across some ninety cities on the continent. The idea is credited to Robert Herries, a well-travelled Scottish banker who understood how exposed a traveller carrying gold or bills of exchange was to theft on the road.

The scheme let a customer deposit money in London and draw it back out from a partner house abroad, without carrying coin across borders. It never became widely popular in its own time; the format that stuck was Thomas Cook's circular notes of 1874, and it took American Express, in 1891, to make traveller's cheques a mass product.

FTX, once the world's second-largest cryptocurrency exchange, collapsed within days in November 2022 after reporting revealed that founder Sam Bankman-Fried had secretly funnelled billions of dollars in customer deposits into a sister trading firm, Alameda Research. A wave of withdrawal requests the exchange could not meet exposed the shortfall almost overnight.

FTX filed for bankruptcy on 11 November 2022, and roughly eight billion dollars in customer funds turned out to be missing or misused. Bankman-Fried, once compared in the press to a young J.P. Morgan, was convicted of fraud and conspiracy in 2023 and sentenced to twenty-five years in prison.

In January 2021 members of the Reddit forum r/WallStreetBets noticed that hedge funds had bet heavily against GameStop, a struggling video game retailer, by short selling more shares than technically existed. Buying in coordinated waves, the traders drove the stock from under twenty dollars to nearly five hundred within days, forcing short sellers to buy back shares at any price to limit their losses.

Melvin Capital, one of the funds caught short, needed an emergency cash injection to survive, and trading app Robinhood briefly froze purchases of the stock, drawing a congressional hearing over whether it had acted to protect Wall Street rather than its own users. The episode became a lasting example of retail traders moving a market that institutions had assumed was theirs alone.

Congress passed the Banking Act of 1933, known by the names of its Senate and House sponsors Carter Glass and Henry Steagall, after roughly nine thousand American banks had failed since 1929. The act forced commercial banks that took ordinary deposits to stop underwriting and trading securities, splitting institutions such as J.P. Morgan into separate deposit-taking and investment arms.

It also created the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation, guaranteeing depositors' savings up to a set limit so a rumour alone could no longer start a run. The wall between commercial and investment banking held for over six decades until Congress repealed the separation provisions in 1999, a change some later blamed for widening the 2008 financial crisis.

Prospectors on the eastern slope of Mount Davidson in Nevada had been chasing gold for years before they realised the heavy blue-grey clay clogging their pans was, in fact, richer in silver. Henry Comstock claimed a share of the ground and gave the lode his name, though he sold his interest cheaply and missed most of the fortune.

The Comstock Lode became the largest silver deposit found in North America, and its output was rich enough in gold too that estimates put the split near three-fifths silver to two-fifths gold. Virginia City boomed around it, a US mint opened at nearby Carson City within a decade, and the flow of silver helped push Nevada to statehood in 1864.

Isaac Newton spent his later career as Master of the Royal Mint, a post that had nothing to do with physics but paid well and mattered to the crown. In September 1717 the Treasury asked him to explain why gold kept flowing into England while silver flowed out to India, and his report set the price of the gold guinea at twenty-one shillings.

Newton had priced silver too cheaply relative to gold at that rate, so silver coins kept being melted down or shipped abroad rather than spent at home, leaving gold as the metal actually circulating in England. He had not set out to choose a monetary system: the guinea's price simply pushed the country onto a gold standard by accident, one that lasted, with wartime interruptions, into the twentieth century.

Muhammad Yunus, an economics professor at Chittagong University, began in 1976 by lending small sums out of his own pocket to villagers in Jobra who could not get loans from any bank because they had no collateral to offer. His first loans, reportedly under thirty dollars split among dozens of basket weavers, freed them from middlemen who had been taking most of their profit.

The experiment grew into the Grameen Bank, formally chartered in 1983, built on group lending and near-total repayment from borrowers with no credit history at all. Yunus and the bank shared the 2006 Nobel Peace Prize for the model, which spread to dozens of countries even as later critics questioned how much it actually lifted borrowers out of poverty.

In late 2009 Greece's incoming government revealed that the country's budget deficit was far larger than previous figures had shown, and ratings agencies began cutting its credit rating within months. By spring 2010 Greece could no longer borrow affordably on open markets and needed the European Union and IMF to step in with the first of several bailouts.

The rescue loans came tied to deep spending cuts and tax rises that shrank the Greek economy by roughly a quarter over the following years and pushed unemployment above 25 percent. Fears that Greece might leave the eurozone entirely, and take the currency's credibility with it, kept the crisis at the centre of European politics for most of the decade.

Thomas Gresham did not coin the phrase that carries his name. In a 1558 letter to the newly crowned Elizabeth I, the queen's financial agent explained why English coinage was in such poor shape: Henry VIII and Edward VI had debased the currency, cutting the silver content of coins while keeping their face value the same.

Gresham's point was that good and bad coin cannot circulate together, because people hoard or melt the coins with more real silver and spend the debased ones first. The economist Henry Dunning Macleod named this bad money drives out good after Gresham three centuries later, in 1857, long after Gresham himself was dead.

A merchant in Basra who wanted to pay a supplier in Cairo did not need to send coin overland through bandit-prone country. He could hand cash to a broker in Basra, who sent word to a partner broker in Cairo, who paid out the equivalent sum on the strength of that word alone. By around 800, this network of brokers, known as hawala, was moving money across the Abbasid caliphate without moving any of it physically.

The system ran on trust between brokers who settled their own balances later, sometimes in caravans of goods rather than coin, and on records that were often no more than a coded note. It still operates today, largely unchanged in principle, and remains one of the main ways money crosses borders in parts of South Asia, the Middle East and East Africa where formal banking is scarce.

Umayyad caliph Abd al-Malik reformed the gold coinage around 696, minting dinars in Damascus that dropped any image of a ruler. Earlier Arab coins had borrowed portraits from Byzantine and Sasanian models; the new dinar carried only Quranic inscriptions in kufic script, a deliberate break from the coinage of the empires the caliphate had displaced.

Each dinar weighed one mithqal, about 4.25 grams of gold, and the standard held steady enough that dinars from Damascus, Cairo and later Baghdad were interchangeable for centuries. Abd al-Malik paired it with a silver dirham reform the same decade, giving the caliphate its own currency system independent of Byzantine and Persian coin for the first time.

By late 1989 the grounds of the Imperial Palace in Tokyo were said, on paper, to be worth more than the entire state of California, and the Nikkei stock index had multiplied several times over in a few years on cheap credit. The Bank of Japan began raising interest rates that December to cool the speculation, and the index started sliding almost immediately.

Property prices took longer to give way but fell just as hard through the early 1990s, leaving banks holding loans against collateral that was no longer worth what it once was. The stagnation that followed lasted so long that Japanese economists came to call the years after it the lost decade, and the phrase eventually stretched to cover two.

Kublai Khan made paper notes, called chao, the empire's enforced currency after founding the Yuan dynasty, backed by government reserves of silk and precious metal rather than by coin in circulation. Refusing the notes for payment could carry the death penalty, a coercion Marco Polo, visiting the Mongol court in the 1270s, described with evident astonishment.

Polo wrote home that the paper was made from the bark of mulberry trees, pounded into pulp and stamped with an official seal, and that it passed for gold and silver throughout the khan's dominions. The system worked while the Yuan state controlled supply carefully, but later overprinting drove serious inflation and helped erode confidence in the dynasty by its final decades.

Edward Lloyd's coffee house first appears in print in a London Gazette notice of 21 February 1688, when it stood on Tower Street. There was nothing unusual about the venue itself: London had dozens of coffee houses, each drawing a particular trade to gossip and do business over the same tables day after day. Lloyd's happened to attract shipowners, merchants and the men willing to insure their cargoes.

Underwriters rented boxes, literally tables, where they wrote their names beneath a share of a voyage's risk in exchange for a premium, spreading a single ship's danger across several backers. Lloyd printed shipping news to keep his customers informed, and by 1692 the business had outgrown Tower Street for larger premises on Lombard Street. The coffee itself was incidental to what became Lloyd's of London.

Safaricom, part of Vodafone, launched M-Pesa in Kenya in March 2007 to let people send and store cash using nothing more than a basic mobile phone and a network of small shops acting as tellers. The name fuses mobile with pesa, the Swahili word for money, and it was built for a country where most adults had a phone but no bank account.

Within a few years M-Pesa was handling a share of Kenya's economy that dwarfed anything a mobile payment system had managed elsewhere, letting migrant workers send wages home instantly instead of by bus. It became the template cited whenever mobile money is credited with reaching people that conventional banking in Africa had never bothered to serve.

NASDAQ opened for trading on 8 February 1971, run by the National Association of Securities Dealers to replace the old over-the-counter market, where dealers had quoted stock prices to each other by phone with no central record. It began as a quotation system, not a trading floor: brokers still called each other to execute deals, but every dealer could see the same prices on screen at once.

The absence of a physical floor let it list companies that other exchanges considered too new or too small, which is why technology firms gravitated to it early. Apple, Microsoft and Intel all listed on NASDAQ rather than the New York Stock Exchange, and by the 1990s it had grown into the second-largest stock market in the world by dollar volume.

The agreement was twenty-four brokers signing their names on a single sheet of paper on 17 May 1792, promising to trade only with each other and to charge a fixed commission. They met outdoors because Wall Street had no dedicated trading hall yet, and a buttonwood, a type of sycamore, happened to be growing near the corner of Wall and William Streets.

The pact was meant to shut out auctioneers who were undercutting brokers on price. It set a minimum commission of a quarter of one percent and gave preference to fellow signers. The group moved indoors to a coffee house within months, adopted a formal constitution in 1817, and only later took the name New York Stock Exchange.

On 10 May 1837, every bank in New York City stopped paying out gold and silver for its paper notes, and banks across the country followed within weeks. The panic followed years of speculative lending on land and cotton, tightened further by President Andrew Jackson's Specie Circular, which had demanded gold or silver for federal land purchases instead of paper.

Cotton prices collapsed, hundreds of banks failed, and unemployment in cities such as New York reportedly reached a third of the workforce. The depression that followed dragged on for roughly six years, one of the longest downturns in American history before the Great Depression, and it dominated the single term of Jackson's successor, Martin Van Buren.

The panic began with a failed attempt to corner the market in United Copper stock, which brought down the Knickerbocker Trust Company when depositors learned its president was tied to the scheme and lined up to withdraw their money. Knickerbocker suspended payments on 22 October 1907, and the run spread to other trust companies within days.

There was no central bank to step in, so J.P. Morgan personally organised the response, locking bankers in his library until they agreed to pledge money to prop up weaker firms. The episode exposed how much the financial system depended on one private banker's judgment, and it drove Congress toward the inquiry that produced the Federal Reserve Act six years later.

PayPal began in 1998 as Confinity, a Palo Alto startup building security software for handheld devices before pivoting to letting people beam money between Palm Pilots. The consumer version that let anyone email cash to anyone else launched the following year and found its real audience among strangers trading on a young auction site called eBay.

eBay sellers adopted it faster than eBay's own payment tool, and eBay eventually bought PayPal outright in 2002 rather than keep competing with it. The service normalised paying a stranger over the internet without exchanging bank details, a habit that later underwrote app-based payments far beyond auctions.

Darius I introduced the daric around 515 BCE, an 8.4-gram gold coin stamped with an archer kneeling or running with bow and spear. Persia's empire stretched from Egypt to the Indus, and a coin of fixed weight and purity let tribute, soldiers' pay and long-distance trade all be reckoned in the same unit across that entire span.

The design stayed almost unchanged for close to two centuries, through successive Achaemenid kings, which is part of why it circulated so widely. Greek writers used the archer coin as a byword for Persian gold itself, and hoards of darics turn up from the Balkans to Afghanistan, tracing routes of tribute, mercenary pay and trade.

The Phoenicians had no empire in the usual sense, only a string of independent city-states, Tyre, Sidon and Byblos among them, tied together by ships. From around 1000 BCE those ships carried a purple dye pressed from murex snails, cedar timber, glass and worked metal to markets from Cyprus to Spain, and founded colonies, including Carthage, to secure the routes.

Their most durable export was not a good at all. The Phoenician alphabet, a script of about 22 consonant letters built for recording cargo and prices quickly, was adopted and adapted by the Greeks, who added vowels, and from there passed into the Latin alphabet this sentence is written in.

Finance ministers from the United States, Japan, West Germany, France and Britain met at New York's Plaza Hotel on 22 September 1985 and agreed to push the dollar down against the yen and the deutsche mark. American exporters had been squeezed for years by a dollar that made their goods expensive abroad, and Washington wanted its partners to help correct it.

Central banks sold dollars in coordinated intervention, and the currency fell sharply over the following two years. The yen's rise is often blamed for cheapening credit in Japan and helping inflate the property and stock bubble that collapsed at the end of the following decade, though economists still argue over how much weight the accord itself deserves.

A Quechua herder named Diego Huallpa is credited with finding silver ore on the mountain of Cerro Rico in 1545, in what is now Bolivia. Spanish colonists moved in almost immediately, and over the following three centuries the mountain yielded something on the order of forty-five thousand metric tonnes of refined silver, worked largely by conscripted indigenous labour under brutal conditions.

The metal crossed the Atlantic in convoy and did not stay in Spain: it paid armies in Flanders, bought goods from China, and pushed Spanish prices roughly threefold higher between 1500 and 1600. A discovery on one Andean mountainside had become the raw material of a European inflation that lasted a hundred years.

Argentarii worked from small booths lining the Roman Forum, taking deposits, extending loans and testing coins for silver content in an economy that ran on many different currencies passing through one city. By the late Republic, around the century marked here, their records were considered reliable enough that Roman courts accepted an argentarius's account book as evidence in disputes over debt.

They also ran the auctions of the day, holding funds in escrow and settling payment between bidder and seller much as an escrow agent does now. The profession outlasted the Republic itself, continuing under the emperors even as the state periodically tried to cap the interest rates a banker could charge.

The aureus was Rome's gold coin, first struck in quantity in the late Republic, around the 40s BCE, and worth roughly 25 silver denarii. At about 8 grams, it was too valuable for everyday market purchases, a soldier's monthly pay ran to only a few of them, and it settled the large transactions ordinary silver coin was too bulky to carry.

Its gold content stayed remarkably stable for over two centuries even as the denarius was repeatedly debased, which made the aureus the coin large estates, senators and the imperial treasury actually trusted for storing wealth. Constantine eventually replaced it with the solidus in 312, a coin built on the same logic of keeping gold honest while silver was let slide.

The denarius that Augustus's soldiers were paid in had been almost pure silver. By the reign of Gallienus around 270 CE, the coin nicknamed the antoninianus that had replaced it was mostly copper with a thin silver wash, the metal squeezed out gradually over decades to stretch a shrinking treasury across wars, plague and rival claimants to the throne.

Prices did not stay still while the coinage thinned. An Egyptian wheat price that had held for generations climbed several-fold within a few decades of the third century, and Diocletian's Edict on Maximum Prices in 301, an attempt to freeze costs by decree, failed to hold. The crisis pushed Rome toward Constantine's more disciplined gold solidus a generation later.

Rome struck its first denarii around 211 BCE, in the middle of the war against Hannibal, replacing an older bronze and silver coinage that had buckled under the cost of fighting Carthage. The name meant containing ten, its original value in bronze asses, and the coin weighed close to 4.5 grams of silver.

The denarius outlasted the war by centuries. It paid Roman legionaries, financed the Republic's conquests and then the Empire's administration, and stayed in production, its silver content slowly cut along the way, until the third century CE. Roman soldiers' pay, the stipendium, was reckoned in denarii for most of that span.

Augustus ran censuses across the Roman world to list who owed what, in property and in tax, replacing the patchwork of local assessments that earlier provinces had used. Officials recorded land, households and citizenship status, and the resulting registers let Rome tax its territories on a common, empire-wide basis rather than province by province.

A census under Augustus is the setting the Gospel of Luke gives for Joseph and Mary's journey to Bethlehem, though historians dispute whether any single Augustan census matches the date or scope the Gospel describes. Whatever the truth of that story, the administrative innovation behind it, reckoning an empire's subjects for tax, was real and endured well into later Roman government.

Mayer Amschel Rothschild sent his five sons from Frankfurt to Vienna, London, Paris, Naples and back home, each running a branch of the same house. The London branch, under Nathan, financed British war spending against Napoleon, and by 1815 the family had a private courier network faster than most governments' own dispatches.

That network is the source of the old story that Nathan learned of Wellington's victory at Waterloo before London's officials did and used the news to trade. The tale is unproven and probably exaggerated, but the underlying advantage was real: the Rothschilds moved information and gold across a fractured, war-torn Europe faster than any state could, which is what let them underwrite loans for Britain, Austria and Prussia alike.

London had no fixed meeting place for merchants until Thomas Gresham built one at his own expense, modelling it on the bourse he had seen in Antwerp. Queen Elizabeth I toured the finished four-storey building on 23 January 1571, gave it a licence to sell wine and beer, and declared that it should be known as the Royal Exchange.

Before this, deals in London were struck in the street or in scattered taverns with no shared record of prices. The Exchange gathered merchants, moneylenders and traders selling everything from spices to lute strings under one roof, and it stayed the City's commercial centre for generations after Gresham's death.

A shekel was not a coin. It was a weight of barley or silver, roughly eight grams, against which a scribe in Uruk or Ur could check that a payment matched what was owed. Coined money was millennia away, so trade ran on weighed metal, verified on scales kept by temples and palaces that acted as the era's clearinghouses.

The word survived the system that produced it. It passed into Akkadian, Hebrew and Aramaic as a unit of weight and later of coined currency, and modern Israel revived it as the name of its own currency in 1980. A measure invented to settle grain debts in Sumer ended up naming a twentieth-century banknote.

Finance ministers from the Group of Ten met at the Smithsonian Institution in Washington on 17 and 18 December 1971, four months after Richard Nixon had suspended the dollar's convertibility into gold. They agreed to devalue the dollar against gold by roughly eight and a half percent, to about thirty-eight dollars an ounce, while other major currencies rose against the dollar by a similar margin.

The deal also widened the band in which currencies could float around their new fixed rates, from one percent to two and a quarter percent either side. Nixon called it the greatest monetary agreement in world history, but it lasted barely a year: renewed pressure on the dollar forced a further devaluation in February 1973, and within weeks the major currencies abandoned fixed rates for good.

The piece of eight was not a pirate's invention but a bureaucratic one. Spain's Pragmatica de Medina del Campo in 1497 fixed the silver real as the kingdom's unit of payment and set the standard for a larger coin worth eight reales, struck to a precise weight of roughly twenty-five and a half grams of fine silver.

That consistency, more than any royal decree, is what made the coin travel. Merchants from Manila to Amsterdam trusted its weight without needing to trust the government that struck it, so it circulated for centuries across Europe, the Americas and Asia, and its fractional divisions later shaped the design of the United States dollar itself.

Spaniards of the mid-sixteenth century did not experience the price revolution as a single event with a date. It was a slow tripling of prices across a hundred years, driven by shipments of Potosi and Zacatecas silver arriving faster than the economy could absorb them, and it is only visible at all because clerks kept records of what bread, cloth and wine cost from decade to decade.

The inflation did not stay inside Spain's borders. Silver paid for imports, so the money supply leaked outward through trade to France, the Dutch Republic, England and the Ottoman Empire, each economy absorbing its own share of the shock. Economists reconstructing the pattern centuries later gave it the name by which it is now known.

Through the mid-2000s American lenders sold mortgages to borrowers with weak credit or no proof of income, betting that rising house prices would let anyone refinance out of trouble. Those loans were bundled into securities rated safe by agencies that, it later emerged, had barely examined what was inside them.

House prices stopped rising in 2006, and defaults climbed fast enough to sink Bear Stearns and, in September 2008, Lehman Brothers, the largest bankruptcy in American history. Credit markets froze worldwide, governments spent trillions propping up banks, and the recession that followed cost millions of jobs across the United States and Europe.

Stockholms Banco, founded by Johan Palmstruch in 1657, lent out the copper coin depositors gave it, which was normal enough until Sweden cut the copper content of its coins in 1660 and depositors rushed to withdraw the old, heavier coins the bank no longer held. Palmstruch's fix, in 1661, was to issue paper notes redeemable for coin, Europe's first banknotes.

The notes solved the immediate cash crunch but removed the discipline that deposits had imposed: the bank could print more of them than it could ever back. Lending outran reserves within two years, the notes lost value, and Palmstruch was imprisoned for the losses. His banking privilege passed in 1668 to what became Sveriges Riksbank, the world's oldest central bank.

Switzerland had protected bank clients informally since a Geneva ordinance of 1713, but the Federal Act on Banks and Savings Banks, passed in February 1934, made disclosure a criminal matter for the first time. Article 47 threatened bankers with imprisonment for revealing client information without consent, turning custom into statute almost overnight.

The timing points to Nazi agents who were hunting for German-owned accounts abroad, though a French scandal that had just exposed undeclared Swiss holdings by politicians and clergy may have mattered as much. Either way, the law gave Swiss banking the reputation for secrecy that later drew wealth, and scrutiny, from across the world.

Congress passed the Coinage Act on 2 April 1792, and George Washington signed into law the first federal building authorised under the new Constitution: a mint, sited in Philadelphia because the city was then the nation's capital. The act named the dollar the country's standard unit and, borrowing the habit from Spanish coinage, divided it decimally into cents, dimes and mills.

The dollar's weight in silver was pegged to the already familiar Spanish milled dollar that had circulated in the colonies for generations, so merchants did not have to learn an unfamiliar unit from scratch. The new mint took almost a year to produce anything: its first coins, 11,178 copper cents, were not struck until 1 March 1793.

The Sixteenth Amendment was ratified on 3 February 1913, overturning an 1895 Supreme Court ruling that had struck down an earlier income tax as an unapportioned direct tax. Congress had already sent the amendment to the states in 1909, and it took the required three quarters of them roughly four years to agree.

The first tax under it, passed later in 1913, was modest by later standards: rates started at one percent and topped out at seven percent on incomes above five hundred thousand dollars, and it applied to only a small fraction of households. The rates and reach both grew sharply once the United States entered the First World War in 1917.

The prestiti began as forced loans. Venice's wealthiest citizens were required to lend the state around half to one percent of their assessed wealth, and many preferred that to ordinary taxation because the state paid five percent interest on it. In 1262 the government rolled these scattered obligations into a single perpetual fund, the Monte Vecchio, rather than repaying anyone.

Because the loans were never redeemed, holders needed another way to get their money out, so a secondary market grew for buying and selling claims on the fund. That market, not the loan itself, is what made 1262 matter: a citizen's forced contribution had become a security that could be traded, priced and passed to someone else entirely.

The Dutch East India Company, chartered in 1602 as the world's first company to issue tradeable shares, let its charter lapse on 31 December 1799 after decades of smuggling, corrupt officials and wars with Britain had left it insolvent. War with Britain after 1780 had wrecked its shipping and trade just as competition from other European companies was already eating into its profits.

The Batavian Republic, the French-backed government then ruling the Netherlands, absorbed the company's remaining debts and its colonial territories in Asia, chiefly the Indonesian archipelago. Those possessions became the direct foundation of the Dutch East Indies, a colony the Netherlands would govern for another century and a half.

By late 1923 the German mark was losing value by the hour, not the day. Prices in restaurants rose between courses, workers were paid twice a day so they could spend wages before lunchtime shopping got more expensive, and the exchange rate against the dollar reached roughly 4.2 trillion marks by November.

Banknotes lost real value faster than mints could print new denominations, so some notes were overprinted with extra zeros to keep pace. People reportedly burned bundles of cash for warmth because it was cheaper than buying firewood with it. The crisis ended when a new currency, the Rentenmark, was introduced in November 1923, backed by mortgages on land and industry rather than gold.

Western Union had spent the 1860s stitching together a transcontinental telegraph network, and by 1871 it had the wires and the branch offices to try something new: moving money itself, not just messages about it. A customer handed cash to a clerk in one city, who wired the details to a clerk in another, who paid it out to the recipient there.

The service meant money that once took days by mail or stagecoach could arrive within the hour. It became the company's second identity alongside the telegram, and it outlived the telegram entirely: Western Union stopped sending wires in 2006 but is still moving money for customers today, now mostly online rather than over copper lines.
